content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.texts-public-domain-native-american-southwest-project-gutenberg-the-sia-stevenson-md-l24509-l24589","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/native-american-southwest/project-gutenberg/the-sia-stevenson.md","passage_locator":{"label":"HEYOKA. / DOR8EY.1 THE HEYOKA GODS. 469 / HEYOKA FKAST. / STORY OF A HEYOKA MAN.; lines 24509-24589","start":"24509","end":"24589","translation":"the-sia-stevenson","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"A human Heyoka man foreknows that he and his horse will die at the first thunder of the next spring. He marks himself and the horse with zigzag clay lines, walks near camp singing with a pipe pointed skyward, and repeats these actions when the first thundercloud appears. A storm comes with wind, rain, lightning, and thunder; after it passes, the people find that the man and horse have been killed and burned by the Thunder-beings, especially at the marked places. The passage closes by linking former foreknowledge with the rule not to reveal a personal wakan mystery.","language":"English with transcribed song terms","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The passage says people of former times knew when they were about to die and dreamed about their deaths.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"One man said that when the first thunder was heard the next spring, he and his horse would die.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The man's kindred wept from time to time because of his announced death.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The man decorated the horse's legs, neck, and back with light gray clay zigzag lines, and made similar lines on his own arms.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The man walked on the prairie near the camp while singing and holding a pipe with its stem pointed toward the sky.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"When the first thundercloud appeared in spring, the man said this was the day he was to die.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"On that day he tied the horse's tail in a rounded form, placed a scarlet blanket around its neck, spread a fine blanket over fire.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"An Aiiiigg-ite or Two Faces takes a child from its parents, uses a rose brush on the child's face the Anuijg-ite, do not know where it lives, do not follow it, and avoid going outdoors at night.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The Anuijg-ite can runs crying around the lodge, becomes silent, and cannot be found by his parents or by people in a neighboring camp.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The mother later hears a voice repeating that she told a ghost to take the child, along with the rattling of small bells.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The mother plans to with traces of a hearth cult.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The Black Bear people are associated with ground or earth, Small Bird people with Thunder-beings Tokonabi.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Tokonabi is located, as far as the author can learn, near the junction of the Little Colorado and Great Colorado in It describes Patun/Squash, Lenya/Flute, Patki, Piba, and related clans; discusses the southern origin and transmission of the Alosaka cult; and notes ritual objects and images including horned figurines, pollen or flower mounds, Alosaka personations, the Tuwapontumsi shrine with petrified wood, and Alosaka images in New-fire and Winter-solstice contexts.","language":"English, with Hopi/Tusayan terms","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The passage states that Little Colorado pueblos were settled by clans from the far south, or Palatkwabi.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Some clans from the Little Colorado area are said to have gone northward to Hopi pueblos, while others went eastward to Zuni.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The Patun or Squash clans are described as among the first clans to migrate from Little Colorado pueblos in search of homes in northern Tusayan.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The Patun/Squash clans are said to have been accompanied by Atoko/Crane and Kele/Pigeon-hawk clans.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The Patun/Squash migrants made a settlement at Tcukubi, later abandoned it, and moved to Old Mishongnovi; some also south.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The Alosaka personation is described as prominent in the Flute observance at related Flute clans.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"At Walpi, the continued practice of Alosaka ceremonies is said to have fallen to Asa and Honani clans after woman.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The Tuwapontumsi shrine is described as containing no statue, only a block of petrified wood.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"A two-horned figure called Tuwapontumsi is described as a female complement of the double-horned MIGRATION TRADITIONS / TUSAYAN MIGRATION TRADITIONS / TUSAYAN MIGRATION TKABITIONS / CLANS FROM PALATKWABI AND THE LITTLE COLORADO; lines 1303-1388","start":"1303","end":"1388","translation":"tusayan-migration-traditions-fewkes","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage describes traditions and historical inferences concerning Patki clans, their southern origin at Palatkwabi, a flood-driven northward migration attributed to Paluliikon the Great Snake, their settlements along the Little Colorado and at Pakatcomo, their rain rites performed for drought-stricken Walpi, and later movement toward Walpi under pressure from raiding and settlement abandonment.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The designation \"Patki clans\" includes a southern refuge-seeking group among the Hopi, including Lizard/Sand, Rabbit, Tobacco, and Rain-cloud clans.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The Patki clans are said to have once lived on the Little Colorado near Winslow and, after entering the Walpi valley, built and occupied Pakatcomo.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The original home of the Patki clans is named Palatkwabi and is placed near San Carlos in the Gila valley of southern Arizona.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Patki legends say their ancestors were forced to leave their ancient home because of destructive floods attributed to Paluliikon, the Great Snake, and then migrated northward through a series of pueblos.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The named migration route includes Kuiichalpi, Utcevaca, Kwinapa, Jettipehika or Tciibkwitcalobi/Chaves pass, Homolobi, Sibabi, and Pakatcomo.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Three early Patki village names, Kwinapa, Utcevaca, and Kufichalpi, are described as not yet identified, and Anawita, chief of the Patki, is said to be able to point them out.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"When the Patki arrived in Tusayan they built Pakatcomo, and some later went to the Middle mesa and others to Walpi.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Patki traditionists say the Walpi people were distressed by lack of rain and crop failure and invited the Patki to perform rites to relieve the calamity.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The Patki societies accepted the invitation, erected altars, and sang rain songs at Tawapa; afterward mist appeared, followed by heavy rain with thunder and lightning.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The rain and thunder frightened Walpi women, while 2001-2169","start":"2001","end":"2169","translation":"tusayan-migration-traditions-fewkes","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage discusses evidence for long Hopi residence in Tusayan, compares Eototo with Masauu, lists Kokop and Honani clan members, describes Tewa and Tano migrations from the Rio Grande to Hopi country and partial return, and recounts Honani traditions about katcinas emerging from the Underworld at Tuwanacabi, being kept by Honani clans, and later clan movements and dispersals after the Awatobi massacre.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The pictography and pottery of Sikyatki are described as distinctly Hopi, unique in the Pueblo area, and evidence for long residence in Tusayan.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Eototo is said to have many resemblances to Masauu and may be the same being under another name.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The passage states that there was formerly an Eototo clan among the Kokop people and that the masks of the two personifications are very similar.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"In Niman-katcina, where Eototo is personated, the Kokop chief assumes that part.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"During the late seventeenth century, many clans, mainly Tewa people and some Tano people, fled from the upper Rio Grande valley to Hopi country.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Around the middle of the eighteenth century, many descendants of these fugitives were persuaded to return and were reestablished in new pueblos.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The passage characterizes the movement as a wave of migration from the Rio Grande to Hopi country followed by a return of the same people to their former homes.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Many Tewa people who fled to Tusayan are said never to have returned, and this is used to explain the presence of many Tanoan ceremonies in Hopi pueblos, especially on the East mesa.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"No connected migration story of the Honani clans had been obtained, but they are said to have lived at Kicuba and to have brought katcinas now in their special keeping.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The Honani clans are said to have once lived at Tuwanacabi, north of the Hopi pueblos, where ruins are still visible.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The Honani say that the Honani katcinas came up from the Underworld at Tuwanacabi and entrusted themselves to the special keeping of these clans.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The Honani migrated from Tuwanacabi to Oraibi, and later some went to content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.texts-public-domain-native-american-southwest-project-gutenberg-tusayan-migration-traditions-fewkes-md-l2365-l2532","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/native-american-southwest/project-gutenberg/tusayan-migration-traditions-fewkes.md","passage_locator":{"label":"CLANS FEOM MUIOBI / CLANS FROM MUIOBI / TUSAYAN MIGBATION TEADITIONS / CLANS FROM MUIOBI; lines 2365-2532","start":"2365","end":"2532","translation":"tusayan-migration-traditions-fewkes","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage discusses Pakab ritual connections with Zuni warrior societies, possible Pakab-Awata relations to Awatobi, and traditions of Asa/Tcakwaina clan migrations from the Rio Grande region through several pueblos to Zuni, Awatobi mesa, East mesa, Canyon de Chelly, Walpi, and Sichumovi. It also correlates some Asa traditions with drought, famine, Anza-era reports, and post-1680 Tanoan movements.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A Pakab chief is described as also chief of a warrior society called Kalektakii, which Hopi identify with the Zuni Society of the Bow.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The Pakab chief has a figurine of Piiukonhoya corresponding to the Zuni Ahaiuta, and his acts when setting it in place are described as identical with those of Naiuche, the Zuni Bow chief.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The room where the figurine is kept has wall figures of animals of the cardinal points, and the passage says these are identical with those at Zuni.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The public dance of the Momtcita is said to resemble the War dance at Zuni.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The passage states that evidence indicates the Momtcita is closely related to the warrior celebration of Zuni Bow priests and may have been derived from Zuni, a Zuni pueblo colony, or the same source as the Zuni variant.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The passage treats the Pakab or Reed/Arrow clans as possibly the same as the Awata or Bow clans and as possible founders of Awatobi, while noting limited evidence.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The Asa clans are said to have formerly lived near Santa Fe and Abiquiu, to have Tewa ancestry, and to have left the Rio Grande around the end of the sixteenth century.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The Asa migration route is described as going to Tukwi, then Kawaika, Akokaiabi, and Sioki/Zuni, where some clan members still lived as the Aiwakokwe clan.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Some Asa continued from Zuni to the Awatobi mesa, built Tcakwainaki, and were said to have katcinas with them.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The Asa did not remain long at Tcakwainaki and continued to the East mesa, where some traditions say they joined related Tewa clans and aided them in fights with the Ute.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Asa traditions say they later built houses at the end of the East mesa above the gap east of Hano.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Years of drought caused famine, after which the Asa moved to Canyon de Chelly in the Navaho country, lived in houses now ruined, intermarried with the Navaho, and eventually returned to Walpi.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"After the Asa returned to Walpi and found other Tewa clans in their former dwellings, the Walpi chief assigned them a new village site at the head of the Stairway trail on condition that they defend it against enemies.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Toward the end of the eighteenth century, most women of the Asa phratry moved to another point on the East mesa and founded Sichumovi.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The passage suggests the Asa Anza.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The passage says it is not unlikely that Asa and Tewa clans formed part of Tanoan people who left the upper Rio Grande valley after the 1680 rebellion and traveled to Tusayan by way of Zuni.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Pakab It then summarizes East Mesa ritual calendars for Walpi, Sichumovi, and Hano, emphasizing Walpi's modified Hopi ritual, Sichumovi's eastern pueblo and Zuni-related elements, and Hano's fragmentary Rio Grande/Tcewadi ritual survival with katcina personations visiting kivas.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The Sumaikoli priests and cult are described as closely connected with the katcinas and as supposed to have been introduced into Tusayan from New Mexico.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Walpi is identified as the only East Mesa pueblo where a true Hopi ritual is celebrated, while also being strongly affected by intrusive clans from other stocks.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The Powamu observance at Walpi is said to differ greatly from the Oraibi performance, with Asa and Hano clans named as especially important in producing the modification.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The Walpi ritual calendar lists observances across the year, including Winter Snake or Flute, Powamu, Palulukonti, Sumaikoli, abbreviated katcina observances, Niman-katcina, Tawa-paholawu, Snake or Flute dance in alternate years, Lalakonti, Mamzrauti, Wiiwiitcimti or Naacnaiya, Soyaluna, and Momtcita.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"A note ascribes the introduction of Natacka at the Walpi Powamu ceremony to the Tcaliwaina or Asa clan.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The Sichumovi ritual calendar includes Pamu'ti, Zuni Return Katcina, Powamti with katcina visitors to Walpi kivas, Palulukonti, abbreviated katcina observances, occasional Sio Calako, occasional Bulintikibi, occasional Owakulti, and a December Soyaluna contribution to Walpi.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"In Sichumovi, Tewa clans identified as Asa and Honani predominate, and katcinas are said to predominate there.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The Bulintikibi at Sichumovi is described as intrusive and almost identical with an eastern pueblo ceremony, while the Sio Calako is described as an incorporated and greatly abbreviated Zuni observance.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The Hano ritual calendar includes abbreviated katcina observances, Powamti katcina visitors to Walpi kivas, Palulukonti, Tawa-paholawu as sun prayer-stick making, Sumaikoli, occasional Howina, Tantai as winter solstice rites, and a warrior celebration.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The Hano ritual is described as a fragmentary survival of the ritual at Tcewadi, the Rio Grande home of the On a mountain the brother embraces his sleeping sister, leading to the birth of ten children, a change of language, and later the creation of rivers, a lake, a village in the lake depths, and mountains. Children from the Wood fraternity are dropped into water, transformed into water animals, restored in the lake, and become the Council of the Gods, prototypes of priestly and war-god offices. The passage then assigns divine dance identities and residences to Si'wulu'si'wa, his sister, the firstborn, and the nine last-born.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The A'shiwi journeyed for many years from the far northwest, first southward and then eastward.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Kia'kwemosi decided to send two of his children, the youth Si'wulu'si'wa and a maiden, to look for a good place to country.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"At midday the brother found his sister sleeping, embraced her, and she became appearance.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The firstborn child was normal, while the other nine children lacked the seeds of The diminutive divine twins identify Sun as father and Laughing water as mother, are asked to fight, and agree to join the A'shiwi against the enemy blocking the quest for the Middle place of the world.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The A'shiwi travel less than a day's journey from Ko'thlu wala'wa to the place later called The battle narrative then describes the A'shiwi praying and dancing while rain weakens enemy bowstrings. Kow'wituma prays to the Sun Father and learns that Ku'yapali'sa's heart is in her rattle; when the rattle is pierced or struck, she dies, causing her people to panic. The A'shiwi capture the village, release three gods, and the gods return to Ko'thluwala'wa. An alternate version says the Sun Father gives turquoise rabbit sticks to Ma'sai'lema, and one strikes the rattle. text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"An ethnographic description of a fifth-day family rite in which an associate shi'wanni and relatives plant te'likinawe prayer plumes in a melon patch for divine, ancestral, fraternity, rain, agricultural, health, and longevity petitions, followed by fasting and household restrictions.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"On the morning of the fifth day, snow covered the earth, valley, and mesa walls while devotees in bright clothing went to and returned from a sacred mission.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The described party included the male head of the house, identified as an associate shi'wanni, his wife, in-laws, children, other relatives, and the writer.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The associate shi'wanni handed the writer te'likinawe made for her and said she must make offerings such as men make.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The party went to the associate shi'wanni's melon patch, where he made an excavation about 14 inches square and about 14 inches deep using an old saber.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"After corn husks were removed from the te'likinawe and prayer meal was sprinkled in the excavation, participants planted te'likinawe without further formality.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Each man deposited one blue-stick te'likinane to the Sun Father and four black-stick te'likinawe to his ancestors.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The wife's younger brother, as a member of the Great Fire fraternity, planted offerings to Po'shaiyanki, Po'shaiyanki's younger brother or fellow, the Cougar of the North, the Sun Father, and the Moon Mother.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The offering to Po'shaiyanki had a miniature crook attached, described as symbolic of longevity; the other offering had a miniature corn planter bound to it to bring much corn in the coming year.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Some te'likinawe had pendent la'showawe, described as one or more plumes attached to cotton cord; those with la'showawe carried prayers for rains, while those without were for clouds and other things.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Each female, including a child of 4, planted text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"English ethnographic passage describing a ceremonial night in the ki'wi'sine: masked personators, initiated male spectators, enforcement of wakefulness, singing, smoking and popcorn water, watching for the Morning Star, kindling fire by friction, and a procession carrying meal, corn, offerings, firebrands, bows, arrows, and yucca.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Masks deposited by the meal painting are removed and worn by Sa'ya'hlia personators, who appear briefly as warriors in the village streets and then return to the ki'wi'sine.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The personators of Shits'ukia and Kwe'lele wear their masks throughout the night and move continually without taking seats.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The personator of Pau'tiwa appears after dark; his mask is removed and placed by the meal painting while he sits behind it between men of the Dogwood and Sun clans.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Male spectators who have passed voluntary initiation are permitted to enter the ki'wi'sine.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Sa'ya'hlia, Shits'ukia, and Kwe'lele whip those found dozing or attempting to leave; no one may sleep or leave before morning.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Members of the Great Fire fraternity and of the He'iwa ki'wi'sine alternate in singing with rattle and drum accompaniment.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"There is constant smoking, popcorn water is drunk, and no grease-contaminated article may be used to dip the water.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Songs and dancing continue until the Morning Star appears, watched for by men who ascend a ladder to the hatchway.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Kwe'lele and the director of the order of Kok'ko 'hlan'na make fire by friction with text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage describes a Zuni ceremonial sequence at Ku'shilowa and in the ki'wi'sine: firebrands and meal are arranged, plume offerings are buried, prayers ask for rain, snow, warmth, crops, seeds, and clothing, household sweepings and ashes are deposited in fields with prayers for their return as food, named figures dance and remain in the ceremonial house, the fire tender is washed for purification and longevity, and te'likinawe are presented to designate persons for ritual offices and divine personation.","language":"English with Zuni terms","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The party proceeds to Ku'shilowa, where the fire tender and Kwe'lele place burning brands, the Ko'pekwin runs a meal line between them, and participants take specified positions facing east.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Those grouped at the back sprinkle meal on the gods and draw in the sacred breath.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The te'likinawe are deposited in a circular excavation made by Pau'tiwa's ceremonial father; the fire tender separates his corn from them, and the father covers the offerings with earth so that no trace remains.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Plume offerings are made to named sacred recipients, and prayers ask for rain, snow, warmth from the Sun Father, abundant fruits and seeds from mother earth, and raiment.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"After the party leaves the ki'wi'sine, families clean their houses; female family members deposit sweepings and ashes with live coals in fields, address them as returning in one year as corn or meal, sprinkle meal, and pray.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The te'likinawe associated with household sweepings and ashes are kept for ten days and then deposited in the fields.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"After the party returns to the ki'wi'sine, the Great Fire fraternity sings with rattle and drum while the four Sa'ya'hlia, Shits'ukia, and Kwe'lele dance until after sunrise.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Kwe'lele brings his extinguished firebrand back to the ki'wi'sine and later deposits it on the road to Ko'thluwala'wa.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"A paternal aunt or woman of the father's clan washes the fire tender's head with yucca suds and bathes his body for purification and longevity, with the stated aim that he may not die but sleep and awake in Ko'thluwala'wa.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The pe'kwin selects giver.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Presentation of te'likinawe indicates that chosen persons must go to the ki'wi'sine; the named appointments include several clouds.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"At night, prayer songs are offered to Beast Gods, Ku'pishtaya, u'wannami, and Pa'yatamu, accompanied by rattle and Water is apportioned, consecrated, mixed with meal, root, and fetishes, whipped into cloud-like suds, and sprinkled with eagle plumes. It also describes choir rehearsals and dawn assembly positions.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The passage enumerates ceremonial participants for two sides, including directors, dancers, water-sprinklers, a Frog clan man, a plume-waver, Corn Maiden personators, a corn symbolizer, singers, a drummer, and flutists.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Several listed roles are explicitly described as impersonated by males, females, youths, or A'shiwanni.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The he'kupowanhak'tona, ushiin'ashute, and sho'lipsimonthle'ona must abstain eight days from animal food and salt; the 'kla'punakwe must abstain four days from animal food and salt.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The passage states that if the sunset-dancer virgins are not virgins, the green corn would be destroyed by worms.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The A'shiwanni feast, retire from the Shi'wano\"kia's house at midnight, sleep at home until dawn, and then gather again in her house.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The la'showawe are made from one tail feather and one wing feather of the mountain bluebird, joined at the quill ends in a V shape and wrapped with cotton cord.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Feathers given to men are from the male bird, and feathers given to women are from the female bird.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The elder brother Bow priest brings selected officials and dancers to the Shi'wano\"kia's house.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The pe'kwin presents a la'showanne to each brought participant and speaks a formula asking for a good heart, good thoughts, one tongue, and rain.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The la'showanne is attached to the left side of each recipient's head by cotton cord and a strand of hair.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The la'showawe are later planted in the fields with te'likinawe on the THANKSGIVING FESTIVAL FOR CROPS; lines 11452-11548","start":"11452","end":"11548","translation":"zuni-indians-stevenson","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage describes a Zuni crop-thanksgiving festival held after harvest, organized by the Bow priesthood with participation by other ritual groups. It details the preparation and distribution of color-coded tobacco cigarettes tied to directions, the summoning of young women for dancing, song composition and prayers to the Gods of War, and the gathering of Bow priesthood members with warrior wands symbolizing the heart or seat of life. A plate caption also identifies a cave shrine of Pa'yatamu.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A plate caption identifies idols removed from a shrine for photographing and names the cave shrine of Pa'yatamu.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The O'wixahai'ye ceremony has no fixed date, depends on the harvest, and occurs after crops are gathered.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The ceremony is described as an annual occurrence of the Bow priesthood, with the Ant fraternity also taking part because of its relation to that priesthood.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"After the elder brother Bow priest decides the festival time, he requests a meeting of the first body of A'shiwanni with the scalp custodian and deputy.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The A'shiwanni assemble in the house of the Priestess of fecundity and each makes a reed cigarette filled with native tobacco, painted the color of the assigned region, and wrapped in a corn husk.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The elder and younger brother Bow priests make two additional cigarettes and give them to the scalp custodian and his deputy.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The Kia'kwemosi collects the cigarettes and tells the scalp custodian to find suitable men from each ki'wi'sine to notify people of the festival and select girls for the dance.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The scalp custodian's assistant selects men from the South, East, and Nadir ki'wi'siwe, while the scalp custodian selects men from the North, West, and Zenith.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The scalp custodian and assistant keep their cigarettes at home for seven nights; on the eighth night they take them to their ki'wi'siwe, light them, and all present take a whiff before other cigarettes are distributed.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Selected men notify young women to assemble in the south and west ki'wi'siwe; the girls gather for four nights and dance, but do not sing.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Song-makers compose songs for four nights; the adopted songs give thanks for the harvest and for respite from the Navaho, and prayers are addressed to the Gods of War for the enemy's destruction.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Members of the Bow priesthood gather in their ceremonial chamber, bringing warrior wands and placing ready wands in an Apache basket with feather ends radiating.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The warrior wand has a slat foundation zigzagged to symbolize lightning, colored blue-green, marked with medicine, and covered with eagle plumes and other feathers.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Different wands have distinctive bases or attachments, including red or black cloth, bird feathers, abalone shell, or crystal.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"The wands are usually worn on the top of the head extending backward and are said to symbolize the heart or seat of life.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:16","text":"The elder brother Bow priest places a package of commercial tobacco in the basket containing the plumes.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"A'wan 'Si'ta, called Great Mother and mistress of the ceremonial chamber, grinds meal for the warriors at a mill at the east end of the room.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:18","text":"A note states that O'winahui'ye had been annual until after 1896 and was held in 1902 for the first time in OF THE SECOND DAY / CEREMONIES OF THE SECOND NIGHT / ANNUAL FESTIVAL OF THE SHA'LAKO / MIXOK CEREMONIES; lines 13295-13393","start":"13295","end":"13393","translation":"zuni-indians-stevenson","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage describes preparations for the Zuni Sha'lako festival, including swept streets, ritual excavations, household fires, spectators, masked god personators, restricted mask preparation, punishments for ritual violations, and a 1879 ceremony in which Shu'laawi'si and other Council of the Gods personators deposit prayer plumes and receive meal offerings at He'patina, a shrine described as symbolic of the Middle of the world.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"On the festival day, streets are swept and excavations are made in different parts of town and under the ladder way of each house to be consecrated; loose earth forms a mound beside each opening, and a stone slab is placed west of each excavation.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Fires are blazing in every house, and the narrator states that this denotes an important occasion because firewood is usually used economically.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"House tops are crowded with dressed men and women from Zuni and other pueblos, while Navahos gather on horseback south of the village to see the gods.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The personators of the Council of the Gods and the Sha'lako leave Zuni at the rising of the morning star for A'kohanna ti'nawki, where a fire is lighted and prayers and songs are rehearsed.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Masks and paraphernalia are conveyed under blankets; masks are stripped of plumes when not in use, repainted before being worn, and prepared solemnly with only initiated persons present.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"If someone enters while masks are being prepared, the person is to extend each ankle and arm in sequence to be struck with bunches of giant yucca.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The passage says that unpunished viewing of Sha'lako masks in preparation, Navahos pressing too near, or a personator speaking to a woman may be understood as reasons why a Sha'lako falls while running.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"A Sha'lako personator must not speak to a woman from the time he enters Zuni until he leaves; if he does, four Sa'va'hla each give him four strokes with giant yucca.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The festival takes place in November, on varying days, and the ritual is said to vary little from year to year.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Shu'laawi'si, preceded by his ceremonial father, goes to He'patina, described as symbolic of the Middle of the world, and deposits prayer plumes in the lower chamber of the shrine.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The ceremonial father carries a tray of prayer plumes, a mi'li, and a sacred meal basket, and sprinkles meal.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Shu'laawi'si is described as black-bodied with colored spots and a similarly decorated mask, wearing or carrying a seed-filled fawn skin, rabbits and rats, necklaces, prayer plumes, and an unlighted cedar-fiber firebrand.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Shu'laawi'si sprinkles meal into the six excavations, recrosses the river, and joins the other Council of the Gods personators at He'patina.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"At He'patina the Council of the Gods is met by A'shiwanni, Ko'mosona, Ko'pekwin, and two Ko'pi'lashiwanni, who pray and sprinkle the gods with meal before the god personators deposit prayer plumes in the lower apartment of the shrine.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Zuni townspeople","description":"The village community preparing for the great festival, including people on house tops.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"Visitors from other pueblos","description":"Men and women from pueblos near and far who gather longevity symbol.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Shu'laawi'si returns to the village, preceded by his ceremonial father, and is joined way.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Sa'yatasha and Hu'tutu carry bunches of deer scapulae in the right hand and a bow, arrows, and te'likinawe in the text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage describes implements and ritual procedures for a game called I'yankolo'we: painted wooden cups, a stone ball and disk, medicines, seasonal timing, consultation with a rain priest, preparation of a room with prayer meal, public announcement, selection of players and watchers, and offerings folded into corn-husk packages.","language":"English with Indigenous terms","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Rain priests and theurgists are said to propitiate their gods for their own good, their people's good, and the good of all the world.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The game implements include four quaking-aspen wooden cups, a stone ball, a white-and-black stone disk, and 106 straws.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The cups are painted white with kaolin, with black paint on the bottoms extending up the sides.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The black paint is said to have come from the undermost world and is mixed with water, medicine, and powdered micaceous hematite called star medicine.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The gaming ball is touched with white paint and wrapped in cotton cord, or else the whole ball is painted white.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The passage says the game formerly used four wooden deer with side openings large enough to contain the ball instead of cups.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"I'yankolo'we is played only in January, February, and March, mostly in February, and once begun must continue without interruption to the close.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"A man wishing to play calls at sunset on a rain priest of the West, East, Zenith, or Nadir and is told to return at night with wafer bread, precious beads, and prayer meal.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The rain priest brings out an ancient gaming ball after a female household member sweeps the inner room.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The rain priest makes four parallel north-south lines of prayer meal by the north wall and places the ball midway on the westernmost line for the night.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The rain priest gives the man wafer bread, a corn-husk tobacco cigarette, powdered mythical medicine plant, and a piece of banded gypsum.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"A member of the governor's staff announces from the housetop that the game will be played the following night and names the leader.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The leader selects three associate players and four watchers, described as seers who choose the hidden cups.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The leader and head It also describes Ho'kiamonne and Let-pochiwe game implements and notes that Ho'kiamonne is offered to the Gods of War at the winter solstice and is played for rain.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A player places one cup over a ball, arranges other cups, packs sand around them, lights a husk cigarette, and puffs smoke over the cups while directing the cigarette toward six directions so that rain-makers will send rain on Zuni.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The cup-and-ball game proceeds by watchers touching cups and paying or receiving counted straws according to which touch finds the ball; the players are repeatedly covered by a blanket while the cups and ball are reset.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"A plant bunch remains at the center, the ball is always immediately over that spot, and the cups and sand are moved so that the center cannot be known.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"When the game returns to the first party, the leader speaks to the ball, telling it to go to its mother Ko'hakwa, identified as a nearby planted bead, and not to its father Hli'akwa, identified as Turquoise, and then to return soon.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The game may continue for four or five days, and participants must not sleep, eat, or drink while it continues.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"After the game, the first leader removes all deposits except the black archaic bead, which remains permanently in the ground, and carries the other deposits, the game, wagers, and the rain priest's ball to his home.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The leader places the game, offerings, money, and silver articles in a basket tray, sprinkles prayer meal over the basket and other wagers, and prays to the Gods of War, rain-makers, A'wonawil'ona, and deceased gamesters.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The borrowed game is returned to its owner; offerings are deposited at the shrine of the younger God of War on Corn mountain, the la'showanne is placed in a medicine box, and the rain priest's ball is returned with a string of precious beads.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Ho'kiamonne uses a yucca-ribbon ball and two slender sticks sharpened at one end and passed through corncob pieces with hawk plumes; players throw the sticks at the ball and try to penetrate it.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Ho'kiamonne is described as a precious game of the Zunis, one offered to the Gods of War at the winter solstice, and it is frequently played for rain with sacred meal sprinkled before the ball is placed.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"In rain-playing Ho'kiamonne, the first person to penetrate the ball lifts it by the stick, draws a breath from it, and thanks the gods that the rains are soon to come.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Let-pochiwe uses pencil-like sticks, reeds, a longer reed called the chief, and canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage describes Zuni pueblo house form and construction: terraced stone-and-adobe dwellings clustered around plazas, status-related residence levels, gendered building tasks, children carrying water, roof and entrance structures, internal connections, selenite light openings, chimneys made from cooking vessels, and plastering/whitewashing techniques.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The pueblo is described as terraced, with houses built one upon another so that one roof may serve as the floor or yard of the dwelling above.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The houses are made of stone and adobe and are clustered around plazas, with covered ways and streets also mentioned.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The passage links wealth and official position with residence in lower houses; people of more modest means live above them, and poorer families generally occupy the uppermost stories.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Women are said to delight in house building, especially plastering, and to regard plastering as their special prerogative.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Men lay stone foundations, build walls, and place large roof-supporting logs.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The roof construction sequence includes logs, cross-laid willow boughs, brush, and an earthen covering.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Little girls assist by bringing water from the river in small water vases carried on their heads.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The houses have outer doors, while roof hatchways with ladders serve as additional entrances.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Older entrances are described as circular openings through thick round stone slabs, closed by round stone slabs held with strong pole props.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Interior doors allow much of the older village to communicate internally without going outside the communal structure.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Small wall openings for light are filled with irregular pieces of selenite.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Chimneys are made from perforated cooking utensils stacked and cemented together, and worn-out cooking pots may be stored for later chimney use.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"Exterior and interior walls are covered with reddish-brown earth-and-water plaster applied by hand in semicircles, with water applied from the plasterer's mouth when needed.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"Inner walls are whitened with white clay dissolved in boiling water and applied with a rabbit-skin glove.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Zuni pueblo residents or households","description":"The WITCHCRAFT 399 / WITCHCRAFT 405 / ORIGIN OF THE FRATERNITIES 409; lines 22669-22764","start":"22669","end":"22764","translation":"zuni-indians-stevenson","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage describes procedures for joining Zuni esoteric fraternities associated with Mystery medicine and other orders. It details sacred meal offerings, gifts between novices and fraternity fathers, requirements for joining Fire, Sword, It'sepcho, and Pa'yatamu orders, compulsory initiation rules connected with plumes and meal lines, and symbolic meanings assigned to the et'tone and mi'li, including Earth Mother, rain, vegetation, and life-giving power from A'wonawil'ona. obligatory; the cost of the required gift may cause the person to join another order first.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"A person desiring to join prepares it.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The theurgist carries the sacred meal package at night to one of the compass points, makes an excavation, and sprinkles the contents into it as an offering to the Beast Gods.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The passage notes that sucking to cure disease is not confined to the Zunis and is described as common among aboriginal peoples of the world with minor differences.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The passage notes comparative examples of sand painting or sand design practices in India and mentions Arizona ceramic sprinkling cups and Renaissance powdered-marble table borders.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Anyone acceptable to a fraternity may join the Fire and Sword orders, whose ceremonials are said to be for rains and snows rather than for healing the sick.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The father of the chosen fraternity gives a blanket to a male novice and a woven dress to a female novice.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The It'sepcho order is joined after membership in the Fire and Sword orders unless the person already belongs to Mystery medicine; its fraternity father gives the novice a woman's belt worn by men in ceremonials.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The Pa'yatamu order exists only in the Little Fire and Cimex fraternities and may be joined only by male members of the Mystery medicine order.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"For four days before initiation, each novice wears a fluffy eagle plume attached to the hair.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Accidentally touching a plume-wearing member of the Fire and Sword orders, or stepping on or within meal lines drawn on the ceremonial chamber roof, obliges the offender to join the text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage describes access difficulties faced by the observer in a ceremonial house, then gives a detailed account of a Zuni 'Hle'wekwe ceremonial movement from chamber to plaza: ritual objects are carried by a maiden and clan girls, accompanied by bow-bearing men; prayer plumes are offered for snow; boxes, notched sticks, deerleg bones, meal, corn pollen, a spruce twig, and a prepared basket are arranged; musicians from a specified kiva play notched sticks under the stated control of Beast Gods while the objects and bows are moved in time from dawn until sunrise.","language":"English with Zuni terms","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The observer occupied the upper story of the ceremonial house; We'wha helped detain an old father below and released the observer when he barred her door, while the old man warned that the observer would bring calamity to herself and the household.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The 'Hlem'mosona placed the 'hle'ettone in the hands of a maiden whose hands had been rubbed with sacred meal; the maiden wore ordinary dress, a white embroidered blanket, and bare feet and lower limbs.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Two men, each carrying an archaic bow with arrows in the right hand, accompanied the maiden from the ceremonial chamber to the plaza in single file, with the girl between them.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Four girls in ordinary dress with black blankets over their shoulders joined the procession, each bearing a mu'et'towe belonging to a specified clan.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Members of each et'tone-bearer's household and clan, and members of the 'Hle'wekwe fraternity, were required to offer four prayer plumes to the et'tone for snows, with offerings made to each of the four regions.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Two decorated boxes were placed end to end east of the center of the plaza, with six notched sticks on them, each crossed with a deerleg bone.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:3","ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The a'kwamosi planted a small spruce twig near the southeast corner of the larger box, described as symbolic of vegetation, and sprinkled meal over it while praying for snows and longevity for his people.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"A handleless purple wicker basket made by a female member of the 'Hle'wekwe was filled with finely ground meal, smoothed into a mound, crossed with corn pollen, topped with a white fluffy eagle plume, and deposited under the larger box.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Three men from the O'he'wa ki'wi'sine sat west of the boxes on wadded blankets and played the notched sticks with deerleg bones.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5","ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The music was said to be controlled by the Beast Gods, with the musicians serving merely as their agents.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The musicians wore upper leg skins of bear or cougar over their lower arms while performing the notched-stick music.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The bone movements over the sticks were performed in repeated fourfold patterns and rapid back-and-forth motions.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The songs were described as the same as those sung in the circle dance in the closing scene of the scalp ceremonial, though here their harmony was obscured by the grating noise of bones on sticks.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The et'towe and bows and arrows were moved terms","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A plate caption identifies a basket with meal crossed and encircled with corn pollen as symbolic of the four regions and the whole world.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The maidens hold a 'hlu'sipone in each hand, while the youth holds his mi'li between his hands.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The Mu'waiye advance in coordinated time and are followed by choir members, a drummer, and a choir of about 100 boxes.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"At a Badger clan house, four aged women receive the et'towe; the et'towe are placed in meal-filled flat baskets in a content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.texts-public-domain-native-american-southwest-project-gutenberg-zuni-indians-stevenson-md-l26091-l26184","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/native-american-southwest/project-gutenberg/zuni-indians-stevenson.md","passage_locator":{"label":"TWENTY-THIRD ANNUAL REPORT PL. CXII / SWORD SWALLOWERS / TWENTY-THIRD ANNUAL REPORT PL. CXIII / FEBRUARY CEREMONIAL OF THE 'HLE'WEKWE; lines 26091-26184","start":"26091","end":"26184","translation":"zuni-indians-stevenson","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Ethnographic prose description of the February ceremonial of the 'Hle'wekwe, including variations from the January ceremonial, plaza dances, arrangement of boxes and ritual objects, sword-swallowing acts, prayers toward six regions, a blessing involving fraternity fathers and children, modifications after deaths in 1897, and the connected Kia'la'silo initiation ceremony.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The January ceremonial is said to be repeated in February with slight variation; if no members are to be received, initiation ceremonies are omitted and west-wall decorations are left off.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The described costume includes a white embroidered kilt, white embroidered sash, woman's red belt, and fox skin pendent at the back instead of the January black breechcloth.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The fraternity dances once in the plaza after the early ceremony with the et'towe and then returns to the ceremonial chamber for the morning meal.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"At noon two a'mosi of the circle dance enter the plaza by the western street; one carries a small purple wicker basket of meal and the other carries the tehl'nawe.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The tehl'nawe bearer stands southeast of the boxes; the leader places the basket in his hand, removes notched sticks and bones from the boxes, reverses the boxes, deposits the meal under the larger box, and leaves by the same route.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Three musicians arrive and sit by the boxes before the 'Hlem'mosona enters from the eastern covered way with the original sword and a sword with feathered handle.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The 'Hlem'mosona repeats sword swallowing on a circuit, including repeated swallowing at six points or six regions.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"After the six-region sword swallowing, the 'Hlem'mosona stands before the boxes, waves the swords over them to the six regions, prays, circles the swords over the boxes, brings them to his lips, and inhales what the passage calls the good in them.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The musicians pray aloud during the sword-and-box prayer, while the retired 'Hlem'mosona observes from the western entrance; after the 'Hlem'mosona leaves, the circle dance begins.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Before 2 o'clock the 'Hle'wekwe assemble in the plaza; women carry two eagle-wing feathers in the right hand and a sword in the left, while the most expert female sword-swallower carries a sword in each hand.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"During the third dance, the leader takes swords from his three fraternity children and swallows them in succession; he then runs four swords down his throat, leaves them there briefly, and withdraws them together.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The plaza ceremony closes with the hands.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The fraternity father distributes a pinch of the meal to each woman of his clan.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"At sunrise the tree butt is worked into a sword; the director cuts the first chip with the stone ax, and each maker fashions CXIII / FEBRUARY CEREMONIAL OF THE 'HLE'WEKWE / ORDER OF KOK'KO 'HLAN'NA / CEKEMOXY FOK-TIIK CUKE OK SOKE TIIHOAT; lines 26400-26501","start":"26400","end":"26501","translation":"zuni-indians-stevenson","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"A ceremonial to cure a sore and badly swollen throat","summary":"The passage describes a Zuni curing ceremonial for an invalid with a sore and swollen throat. administer medicine from a bowl.","language":"English with Zuni terms","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The described rite is presented as a ceremonial for curing order.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Male and female order members sit on opposite sides of the room, and blankets create a dressing room for the god chamber below around dusk.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Shits'ukia carries giant yucca and a rhombus; Kwe'lele carries yucca, fire sticks, and an unlighted drum.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Shits'ukia draws lines of meal across portions of the patient's body, and Kok'ko 'hlan'na follows those lines with yucca; Kwe'lele passes around the patient unless chosen by the patient, in which case roles are reversed.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The meal and yucca treatment is applied across the shoulders, waist, knees, back, arms, and upturned palms in repeated ordered movements.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Kok'ko 'hlan'na hole.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"After the initial treatment, the three gods retire behind the curtain, remove their masks, and return to sit; most members relatives.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Around nine o'clock order members return; different male members personate the three gods during the night, while bowl.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"invalid / patient","description":"A young man with a sore and badly swollen throat, placed on a pallet 30427-30524","start":"30427","end":"30524","translation":"zuni-indians-stevenson","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"An ethnographic description of the Zuni Cimex fraternity sun dance: its four-year alternation with the Little Fire fraternity, a belief that original fire was a gift of the Sun Father, the collection and piling of juniper over an offering-filled excavation, preparation of coals, procession and attire of participants, sprinkling with medicine water, and the passage of dancers, including novices, through the coals.","language":"English with Zuni terms","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The ceremonial is described as celebrated once every four years in March by the Little Fire and Cimex fraternities alternately; the passage also reports a belief that original fire was a gift of the Sun Father and was lit by the sun's rays.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The fraternity convenes on March 2 and holds a four-night ceremonial; on the third day ten men bring juniper from woods south of Zuni and deposit it in the ceremonial chamber before it is carried out at the rising of the morning star.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"A circular excavation with a smaller central excavation is made; prayer plumes and medicine are deposited in the smaller excavation and covered with earth before wood is piled in and over it.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The wood pile is burned until coals remain; two Cimex members rake, scatter, beat, gather, brush, and pack the coals into a mound, after which the plaza is swept.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The dancers arrive from the ceremonial chamber to the plaza in single file, led by a woman who stands immediately before the sprinkler.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4","ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The sprinkler is described with special clothing and ornaments; the passage explicitly says that a blue-green band on his kilt symbolizes the vegetation of the world.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Male dancers carry large unpainted gourd rattles, eagle-wing plumes, and corn-husk packages of meal; the two novices carry red and black blankets described as gifts from their fraternity fathers and also carry quantities of prayer line; officials receive, embrace, and pray over participants; prayer plumes, meal, and bread are offered at ant-hills and in the excavation; the group processes back to the village with scalps; the attached.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"After the passage under the hands, the cedar twigs are received by the pa'mosona and an aid and are later laid on the apexes.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"Women's sticks are black and offered to the rain-makers, while men's sticks are red and offered to the Gods of War for the destruction of the enemy.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"Women divide prayer meal with their companions and sprinkle it over the plumes and ant-hills; the women do not speak on this occasion, while the men pray aloud and deposit prayer plumes.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Warriors and then the populace pass over the meal line and under the hands; the passage explains this as stepping over the sacred road of meal to the home of the ants so that they may keep their lives during travel or war.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The pa'mosona deposits wafer bread as a food offering to the ants in the excavation and destroys the mounds by drawing earth procession.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Except for the scalp-kickers, each person carries a bit of cedar bark in the left hand.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The village is encircled four times from right to left in coil fashion until the group reaches the large plaza, where women and children join and four concentric circles are formed.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"In the plaza, the scalp-kickers lift the scalp-bearing twigs with the fear.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:17","text":"At each return to the starting point, participants expectorate on cedar bark and carry it around the head four times from / A'PI'TLASHIWANNI 587 / A'PI'TLASHIWANNI 591 / A'PI'TLASHIWANNI 597; lines 32266-32356","start":"32266","end":"32356","translation":"zuni-indians-stevenson","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"Ethnographic description of A'pi'tlashiwanni ritual procedures: preparation of feathered gourd sprinklers; making, feathering, guarding, and ceremonial placement of wood idols of the elder and younger Gods of War; arrangement of plume wands and other objects on meal paintings; all-night songs, sunrise handling of a divided scalp, and morning assembly of priests and water-bearers.","language":"English with Zuni terms","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The Kia'kwemosi completes prayer plumes and adds fresh plumes to two long-necked gourd jugs fitted with reed sprinklers; the jugs are later placed on a meal painting and carried by water-bearers or sprinklers.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The wood idols of the Gods of War are completed on the eleventh day; U'yuyewi is made by an aged Deer clan member, while Ma'sai'lema and its appointments are made by members of the Bear clan.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Warriors go separately to the two houses and place two prayer plumes upright in the yucca belt around each image.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"At sunset the image of the younger God of War is carried hidden under a blanket to the house of the maker of U'yuyewi, and the two effigies are set near each other facing east.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Additional prayer plumes are added until the idols are almost hidden; the images are guarded until midnight and then carried with their belongings to the warriors' ceremonial chamber.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The pe'kwin receives the images separately with ceremony and stands them beside a meal painting on the west end of the room.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The elder war-god idol is placed on the northwest corner of the painting, the younger on the southwest corner, with each idol's paraphernalia placed behind it and plume wands in line before it.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Plume wands before U'yuyewi include red sticks offered to the Gods of War to destroy enemies of the world and black sticks offered to deceased warriors for rains; wands before Ma'sai'lema are colored for the six regions and are for destruction of enemies of the six regions.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Three po'nepoyanne, a Whlan'na, the Kia'kwemosi's et'tone, the two gourd jugs, and mi'wachi are placed on or near the meal painting, meal line, and cloud symbol.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"An all-night ceremonial is held in the chamber, during which epic songs of the Gods of War are sung.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"At sunrise the pa'mosona removes a divided scalp from its elevated position in the plaza, attaches it to a pole, and plants it in the northwest corner of the plaza.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"A similar meal painting is expected on the north side of the plaza at sunrise, although the observed pe'kwin completed it later in the morning.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"By 9 o'clock the first body of A'shiwanni, except named absent priests, is assembled; the A'shiwanni wear pure white, while the two 'kia'punakwe are elaborately dressed and described as supposed virgins.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"A note states that these images are made only at initiation and at the winter solstice, with different woods selected for the two occasions.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]}],"figures":[{"id":"fig:1","name_or_label":"Kia'kwemosi","description":"Ritual office holder who completes prayer plumes, adds plumes to the two gourd sprinkler jugs, and has an et'tone deposited on the meal painting.","role_refs":["role:1"],"evidence_refs":["ev:1","ev:5"]},{"id":"fig:2","name_or_label":"U'yuyewi","description":"Wood idol identified in the passage as the elder God of War; made by an aged painting.","role_refs":["role:2","role:13"],"evidence_refs":["ev:2","ev:4"]},{"id":"fig:3","name_or_label":"Ma'sai'lema","description":"Wood image identified in the passage as the younger God of War; content.text: {"record_id":"batch.motif.texts-public-domain-native-american-southwest-project-gutenberg-zuni-indians-stevenson-md-l32359-l32445","source_text_path":"texts/public-domain/native-american-southwest/project-gutenberg/zuni-indians-stevenson.md","passage_locator":{"label":"STEVENSON! / A'PI'TLASHIWANNI 587 / A'PI'TLASHIWANNI 591 / A'PI'TLASHIWANNI 597; lines 32359-32445","start":"32359","end":"32445","translation":"zuni-indians-stevenson","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage describes sacred objects of the Bow priesthood, the clan custody of a precious shell, and the ceremonial preparation of a victor and his elder brother through dress, meal transfer, face anointing, black paint, corn pollen, eagle down, arrow points, war gear, and prayer plumes. The passage itself explains parts of the decoration as cloud, rain, vegetation, and prayer symbolism.","language":"English with Zuni terms","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The po'nepoyanne of the Bow priesthood is described as a corn element surrounded by reeds; six reeds are colored for regions and filled with corn grains of six colors and other seeds, while other reeds contain native tobacco.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The po'nepoyanne is covered or obscured with eagle plumes, cotton cloth, cotton cord, shells, and precious beads.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Two po'nepoyanne belonging to the A'pi'tlashiwanni are mentioned: one is carried to battle and the other remains at home.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The su'hlan'na is described as a large shell very precious to the Zunis; its keeper and vice must be of the Badger clan, and its songs are said to be very old and known only to four Badger clan men.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"The victor and his elder brother wear ceremonial clothing and ornaments, including buckskin, an embroidered sash, turquoise earrings, and elaborate necklaces.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The elder brother Bow priest places meal in the belts of the victor and his elder brother, and they carry it to two idol makers, one of the Bear clan and one of the Deer clan.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The elder brother Bow priest anoints the faces of the victor and his elder brother with a paste made from fat of prey animals of the six regions and the rattlesnake; the kia'punakwe add red pigment and micaceous hematite.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The pe'kwin uses a small black polished pottery vase said to contain black paint from the undermost world, and a medicine bag containing corn pollen.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"The pe'kwin paints the lower part of the face black and applies corn pollen to the upper part by stippling; a corn husk protects the black portion during the pollen application.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"After the face painting, a warrior of the Ant fraternity applies eagle down to the chin, upper lip, nose, forehead, and crown using kaolin paste.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The passage states that the decoration symbolizes purity of heart, prayers breathed into plume offerings, rain sent by deceased A'shiwanni, heavy rain clouds, vegetation, lighter clouds, and the clouds of the world.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"The pe'kwin places an arrow point in each man's mouth, where it may not be removed until sunset.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The victor and his elder brother wear a deerskin hood with a plume wand, a war pouch, bow wristlet, war club, quiver, bow, and arrows; each quiver is checked for one arrow for each of the six regions.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The victor and his elder brother take their prayer plumes from the meal painting, and then all owners remove their prayer plumes after each warrior has deposited two.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:15","text":"A note states that the Bow priesthood alone among the Zunis kills the rattlesnake; the rattle is worn as an amulet for protection from enemies, and the snake fat or oil is rubbed on the face so the enemy
