canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage lists southern Road of Day shrine names, describes post-scalp-ceremonial shrine rotation and placement of elder and younger Gods of War idols with prayer plumes and meal offerings, explains seasonal placement rules for rain at winter solstice, and gives notes on associated place traditions: a miraculous flour sack and bread-making grandmother, Ko'loowisi the Plumed Serpent seen above flood waters, a wool-covered mountain, iconography of U'yuyewi/God of War images, an ancient cave shrine, and a crater at Zuni Salt Lake regarded as the present home of the Gods of War.","language":"English with Zuni terms","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The Road of Day section names a southern route or road and a sequence of named mountains or shrines, including Te'wan ko'han o'nan pii'nina, Shi'akia, Eagle's Nest Mountain, Sack of Meal Hanging Mountain, Twin Mountain, Whitewash Mountain, Face Mountain, and Wool Mountain.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"After a scalp ceremonial, the shrines are taken in rotation; the idol of the elder God of War is placed north of the road of day and the idol of the younger God of War south of it.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"The image is set up, prayer plumes are planted in rows on each side at right angles to the image, paraphernalia are arranged, and meal is sprinkled from the idol outward between the prayer-plume lines.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"At the winter solstice and other peaceful rain-oriented occasions, both gods bear the name A'havuta; at this season the elder god is deposited on U'hana yallanne and the younger on To'wa yallanne, because a north-side placement of U'yuyewi would anger the rains and winds and bring too much cold.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"A note says two girls from Shun'te'klaya were gathering grasses for baskets to hold prayer plumes when they met the elder God of War, who invited them to his mountain-top house; there they saw a small sack of flour hanging from a tree, and the grandmother of the gods made a large basket of bread from a very small quantity of flour.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"A note explains Face Mountain by saying the face and head of Ko'loowisi, the Plumed Serpent, were seen above the waters there by the A'shiwi, who were on To'wa yallanne to escape the great flood.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"A note explains Wool Mountain by saying the Gods of War killed many mountain sheep there, and the grandmother swept sheep wool from the house down the mountain side until the mountain was covered with wool.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The plate description identifies U'yuyewi images and associated carved or represented items: hands of the gods, a war club, an earthly arrow, a serrated cloud tablet, a crescent, a full moon opening, a star cross, a lightning arrow, and umbilicus projections.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"One plate shows idols of the God of War removed from an ancient cave shrine in the west wall of To'wa yallanne and placed outside to be photographed.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The passage states that the A'pi'lashiwanni have many shrines dedicated to the Gods of War and gods.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The passage gives a general statement that Zuni gods are visible in heaven, earth, and waters under the earth, and that NGAI-LAO KINGDOM / I4 THE NORTHERN SHANS / THE MAO KINGDOM / THE BABY; lines 1781-1898","start":"1781","end":"1898","translation":"shans-at-home-milne","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"A Shan baby is rich in having two fathers and two mothers.","summary":"The passage describes Shan beliefs and customs surrounding infants: spirit parents guarding the baby, the infant’s early perception of spirits, a thirty-day purification washing at running water, naming rites involving a water-filled pot, gifts, blessings, a sevenfold white thread around the wrist, and later childcare practices.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"A Shan baby is described as having human parents and also a spirit father, Paw-Hpan, and a spirit mother, Meh-Hpan.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"The spirit father and mother are said to watch over the baby as sentinels and keep bad spirits away.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"A baby smiling in sleep is described as a sign that the spirit parents are playing with him.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"The passage says a very young baby sees the spirit world, fairies, elves, sun- and moonbeams, and small spirits riding dust-specks, but ceases to see this world as he recognizes earthly things.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Thirty days after birth, the mother, father, baby, and any attending friend or wise woman go to a running stream for a ceremonial washing.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"At the stream the mother washes herself, her hair, and the baby, and pours water over the hair of her husband and the woman who attended the birth.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"After this washing the mother is described as purified and able to bring bananas and rice to the monastery and resume household duties.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The passage states that lustrations in running water or temple water are considered to cleanse mind and body, and that washing another person’s hands or hair can express gratitude.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"After the ceremonial washing, the parents hold a naming feast and guests drop small gifts, usually coins, into a large earthenware pot filled with fresh water.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"Guests avoid saying the baby is beautiful or big because such praise might bring bad luck, and instead offer blessings to the parents.","category":"speech","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"The water from the gift-filled pot is poured over the baby, and the wise woman places the money in the child’s hands while wishing health, happiness, and freedom from ninety-six diseases.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"An old man or woman markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage describes Shan bodily markings, charms, and adornments: male leg tattooing as a marker of manhood and marriageability; tattoos and implanted metals as protections, love-charms, or wound-averting charms; discs bearing letters that symbolize animals associated with Gautama's previous lives; female dress, leg rings, and hair practices as age/status markers; and the offering of cut hair to an image-house in hope of luxuriant hair in a future life.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Leg tattooing is described as decoration and as a sign of manhood; a youth is not recognized by girls as a marriageable man until his legs show blue markings.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Designs added to the back or arms are described as charms to ward wounds.","category":"relationship","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The discs often bear four engraved letters, each symbolizing a fish scale, monkey, crab, or womanhood.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Girls usually do not tattoo, except when crossed in love, when a small charm may be tattooed on an arm or on the tip of the tongue.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"Girls and women wear tight circles of cane below the knee, which are usually hidden by clothing and may become marriageable woman.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"A baby girl's head is shaved except for a crown tuft; later the rest is cut as a fringe and allowed to grow request that the bride be brought to her husband.","language":"","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Dreams of items or actions such as coins, running water, the worst omen.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"Dreaming of holding the moon in the hand is described as extremely fortunate, and dreaming that one's hair has become white is taken to mean long life.","category":"other","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Before a marriage is completed, remarkable dreams of the bride, bridegroom, and their relatives are narrated to a wise man for judgment as omens of happiness or bad fortune.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"Thursday and Saturday are described as unlucky days for marriage, and weddings do not take place during fasting months or on monthly fast days.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"After a propitious day is chosen, the parents of the young people invite friends to wedding feasts, and guests arrive on the evening before the ceremony.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"On the wedding day the betrothed man and maid bathe in running water near their respective homes and are not expected to see each other until the afternoon ceremony.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"The wedding takes place at the bride's home; the bridegroom's parents are absent because they prepare at their own home to receive the bride.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"Women among the guests gather around cooking-pots at a temporary outdoor fireplace and help prepare food.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"Friends give small gifts of money to the bridegroom, while no one gives money to the bond.","language":"English","quote_policy":"quoted"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"The bride's father refuses the request for his daughter twice, saying he has changed his mind and ceremony.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"The passage reports a comparison from Ibbotson's Panjab Ethnography in which a Kurmi bridegroom is first married to a bed.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:11"]},{"id":"obs:14","text":"The bedding is new and provided by the bride's father; the husband's pillow must be larger and higher than the wife's, and lines 4343-4462","start":"4343","end":"4462","translation":"shans-at-home-milne","notes":"Stable markdown line range generated from canonical text."},"canonical_text":{"quote":"","summary":"The passage describes Shan funeral practices: water offerings, burial-ground rites with monks and water poured beside the grave, occasional rope assistance for the dead person's spirit to journey north to Mount Meru, grave goods and memorial streamers, a seventh-day feast for the dead, special precautions for a woman who dies with an unborn child, burning of lepers' bodies and shelters, special burial of lightning-struck persons, and clothing rules for natural versus sudden or violent deaths.","language":"English","quote_policy":"summarized"},"literal_observations":[{"id":"obs:1","text":"Women offer water in the name of the dead to anyone who may be thirsty.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:1"]},{"id":"obs:2","text":"At the burial-ground, monks precede the bier, men follow it, and women remain kneeling at a distance rather than going to the grave.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:2"]},{"id":"obs:3","text":"Monks recite Buddhist scriptures, and during the final recitation an earthenware bottle full of water is emptied slowly beside the open grave.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:3"]},{"id":"obs:4","text":"After the water-bottle is empty, the coffin is lowered; sometimes it is raised and lowered several times, and a rope is pulled northward to help the dead person's spirit begin its journey to Mount Meru.","category":"sequence","evidence_refs":["ev:4"]},{"id":"obs:5","text":"Implements of trade are not buried with the body, but rice, tea, tobacco, and sometimes a toy for a child may be placed in graves.","category":"object","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:6","text":"After the grave is filled, the bier and canopy are placed above it; most graves have no tombstone and are not visited, while memorial bamboos with streamers are set up near the monastery during festivals.","category":"setting","evidence_refs":["ev:5"]},{"id":"obs:7","text":"On the seventh day after the funeral, another feast is held, and it is generally believed that the dead person's spirit returns, is present, or is aware of the feast.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:6"]},{"id":"obs:8","text":"The death of a Shan woman with her unborn child is described as the greatest misfortune for both families, and her spirit is believed to become a malignant ghost unless precautions are taken.","category":"attribute","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:9","text":"In such a case, the unborn child is removed, and mother and child are wrapped in separate mats and buried without coffins.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:7"]},{"id":"obs:10","text":"The dead woman and baby are lowered through an aperture made in the side wall of the house, and the opening is filled with new mats so that the ghost may not know how to return.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:8"]},{"id":"obs:11","text":"Lepers live in jungle booths or huts; when they die, their bodies are burned under the shelter where they lived, with wood added to destroy both body and dwelling-place.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:9"]},{"id":"obs:12","text":"A person killed by lightning is wrapped in a fine mat, placed standing in a well-shaped grave, and covered at the head with an inverted earthenware pot.","category":"action","evidence_refs":["ev:10"]},{"id":"obs:13","text":"The passage states that Shans profess ignorance about the lightning burial custom, then reports possible medicinal use of the pot and a suggestion by W.
